HOME IMPROVEMENT CONTRACT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Construction, Inc.

HOME IMPROVEMENT CONTRACT — PARTIES, LICENSE, AND PROJECT TERMS
HOME IMPROVEMENT
(Home improvement contract under California Business and Professions Code § 7159)

Homeowner: Jordan Alex Lee
Property Address: 123 Main St, Springfield

Contractor: Acme Construction, Inc.
Contractor's License Number: 123456
Contractor's Business Address: _______________________________________________

Contract Price: $25,000

Description of the Project and Description of the Significant Materials to Be Used and Equipment to Be Installed: _______________________________________________

Approximate Start Date: September 15, 2026
Approximate Completion Date: November 15, 2026

Schedule of Progress Payments: _______________________________________________
The schedule of progress payments must specifically describe each phase of work, including the type and amount of work or services scheduled to be supplied in each phase, along with the amount of each proposed progress payment. IT IS AGAINST THE LAW FOR A CONTRACTOR TO COLLECT PAYMENT FOR WORK NOT YET COMPLETED, OR FOR MATERIALS NOT YET DELIVERED. HOWEVER, A CONTRACTOR MAY REQUIRE A DOWNPAYMENT.

Downpayment (if any): $_______________
THE DOWNPAYMENT MAY NOT EXCEED $1,000 OR 10 PERCENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE, WHICHEVER IS LESS.

Subcontractor(s) will be used on this project: [ ] Yes  [ ] No
If "Yes": One or more subcontractors will be used on this project, and the contractor is aware that a list of subcontractors is required to be provided, upon request, along with the names, contact information, license number, and classification of those subcontractors.

The homeowner or tenant has the right to require the contractor to have a performance and payment bond.

You are entitled to a completely filled in copy of this agreement, signed by both you and the contractor, before any work may be started.

WHEN A HOME IMPROVEMENT CONTRACT IS REQUIRED, AND ITS CORE WRITTEN TERMS AND DISCLOSURES
California's Contractors State License Law defines a "home improvement contract" as an agreement — oral or written, in one or more documents — between a contractor and a homeowner (or, in some cases, a tenant) for a home improvement as statutorily defined, where the aggregate contract price exceeds $500. Once that threshold is met, the contract and any changes to it must be in writing and signed by the parties before work covered by the contract (or a change order) begins. Before any work starts, the contractor must give the buyer a copy of the signed, dated contract, and the buyer's receipt of that copy is what starts the buyer's statutory cancellation-notice period running. The written contract must include, among other things, the contractor's name, business address, and license number; a "Home Improvement" heading; a "Contract Price" heading with the amount in dollars and cents; a description of the project and the significant materials and equipment involved; headings for the approximate start date and approximate completion date; and, in close proximity to the signatures, a notice that the owner or tenant has the right to require the contractor to carry a performance and payment bond. A change-order or extra-work form becomes part of the contract only if it is a separate writing signed by the parties before the change-order work begins. Beyond these core terms, the contract (or an attachment it references) must include several specific disclosure notices: a commercial general liability insurance (CGL) notice stating, correctly, whether the contractor carries CGL insurance, is self-insured, or carries the liability coverage the law requires; a workers' compensation insurance notice stating whether the contractor has no employees and is exempt, or carries coverage for all employees; a "Mechanics Lien Warning" in specific statutory language, telling the owner that even a contractor who has been paid in full may leave unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, or laborers who can still record a lien on the property; and a notice with the Contractors State License Board's (CSLB) contact information, cautioning the buyer that using an unlicensed contractor may leave the buyer's only remedy in civil court, with possible liability for injuries to the unlicensed contractor or that contractor's employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“home improvement contract” means an agreement, whether oral or written, or contained in one or more documents, between a contractor and an owner or between a contractor and a tenant ... for the performance of a home improvement, as defined in Section 7151, and includes all labor, services, and materials to be furnished and performed thereunder, if the aggregate contract price specified in one or more improvement contracts ... exceeds five hundred dollars ($500)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition of 'home improvement contract' and its $500 price threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "Before any work is started, the contractor shall give the buyer a copy of the contract that is signed and dated by both the contractor and the buyer. The buyer’s receipt of the copy of the contract initiates the buyer’s rights to cancel the contract pursuant to Sections 1689.5 to 1689.14, inclusive, of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(c)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, contractor's duty to give the buyer a signed copy before work starts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "A home improvement contract and any changes to the contract shall be in writing and signed by the parties to the contract prior to the commencement of work covered by the contract or an applicable change order and ... shall include or comply with all of the following: (1) The name, business address, and license number of the contractor."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(d) & (d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, writing requirement and mandatory contractor-identification term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "A notice concerning commercial general liability insurance. ... The notice shall include the heading “Commercial General Liability Insurance (CGL),” followed by whichever of the following statements is both relevant and correct: (A) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) does not carry commercial general liability insurance.” ... A notice concerning workers’ compensation insurance. ... The notice shall include the heading “Workers’ Compensation Insurance” followed by whichever of the following statements is correct: (A) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) has no employees and is exempt from workers’ compensation requirements.” (B) “(The name on the license or ‘This contractor’) carries workers’ compensation insurance for all employees.”"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(1)-(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required commercial general liability insurance and workers' compensation insurance notices (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "Information about the Contractors State License Board (CSLB): CSLB is the state consumer protection agency that licenses and regulates construction contractors. ... Use only licensed contractors. ... If you use an unlicensed contractor, CSLB may not be able to help you resolve your complaint. Your only remedy may be in civil court, and you may be liable for damages arising out of any injuries to the unlicensed contractor or the unlicensed contractor’s employees."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required Contractors State License Board (CSLB) contact and unlicensed-contractor-risk notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when California requires a home improvement contract to be in writing, what core terms it must contain, and what specific disclosure notices it must include — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project or contract. All five citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159) rather than independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent statute rather than five separate ones. This clause doesn't state whether a particular job qualifies as a 'home improvement' as the statute defines that term, whether a particular price aggregates multiple contracts, the exact wording of every notice the statute requires (the mechanics lien warning and CSLB notice are lengthy standardized texts, only partially quoted here), or what content requirement applies to a job that instead qualifies as a 'service and repair contract' under a separate, narrower statute.

DOWN PAYMENT CAP AND THE RULE AGAINST PAYING FOR INCOMPLETE WORK
California law caps the down payment a home improvement contract may require: if any down payment is charged, it may not exceed $1,000 or 10% of the contract price, whichever amount is less, and the contract must display that exact dollar/percentage cap in boldface type. Beyond the down payment, the contractor generally may neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work actually performed or the materials actually delivered — the schedule of progress payments must be stated in dollars and cents tied to specific phases of work, and the contract must include a boldface statement that it is against the law to collect payment for work not yet completed or materials not yet delivered. A contractor who instead furnishes a qualifying performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or an approved joint control is exempt from the down-payment cap and the progress-payment restrictions, and may accept payment before the work is completed. Violating the writing requirement, the down-payment cap, or the rule against accepting payment beyond the value of work performed is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $100 nor more than $5,000, by up to one year in county jail, or by both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“THE DOWNPAYMENT MAY NOT EXCEED $1,000 OR 10 PERCENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE, WHICHEVER IS LESS.”"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(d)(8)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, required boldface down-payment cap statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "(3) If a downpayment will be charged, the downpayment shall not exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or 10 percent of the contract amount, whichever amount is less. ... (5) Except for a downpayment, the contractor shall neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work performed or material delivered."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(a)(3) & (5) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, down-payment cap and prohibition on payment exceeding value of work performed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.5.)
  "A contractor furnishing a performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or a bond equivalent or joint control approved by the registrar covering full performance and payment is exempt from paragraphs (3), (4), and (5) ... A contractor furnishing these bonds, bond equivalents, or a joint control approved by the registrar may accept payment prior to completion."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(a)(8) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, bonded-contractor exemption from the down-payment and progress-payment rules (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.5.)
  "A violation of paragraph (1), (3), or (5) of subdivision (a) by a licensee or a person subject to be licensed under this chapter, or by their agent or salesperson, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000), or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, misdemeanor penalty for violating the writing requirement, down-payment cap, or progress-payment rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual down-payment cap and progress-payment rule for a home improvement contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contract's payment terms. Three of the four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159.5(a) and (b)) rather than independently authored sources; the fourth (section 7159(d)(8)(C)) is a companion section requiring the identical dollar cap to appear as boldface contract language. It doesn't state how 'value of the work performed' is measured in a disputed case, and a contractor who furnishes a qualifying performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or approved joint control is statutorily exempt from the down payment cap, the progress-payment schedule requirement, and the related boldface warnings.

THE THREE-BUSINESS-DAY (OR FIVE-DAY, OR SEVEN-DAY) RIGHT TO CANCEL
Unless a home improvement contract is negotiated at the contractor's place of business, or falls within a narrow set of other exceptions, California law requires the contract to include a "Three-Day Right to Cancel" notice — extended to a "Five-Day Right to Cancel" when the buyer is a senior citizen — allowing the buyer to cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering written notice to the contractor by midnight of the third (or fifth) business day after the buyer receives a signed, dated copy of the contract that includes the notice. If the buyer cancels, the contractor must return anything the buyer paid within 10 days of receiving the cancellation notice. The notice must appear in at least 12-point boldface type, in immediate proximity to the owner's signature space, in the same language principally used in any oral sales presentation, and it must be accompanied by a duplicate, easily detachable "Notice of Cancellation" form. A separate "Seven-Day Right to Cancel" notice applies instead — in place of the three/five-day notice — to a contract for the repair or restoration of residential premises damaged by a sudden or catastrophic event for which a state of emergency or local emergency has been declared.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The notice set forth in subparagraph (B) and entitled “Three-Day Right to Cancel,” or entitled “Five-Day Right to Cancel” for contracts with a senior citizen, shall be provided to the buyer unless the contract is: (i) Negotiated at the contractor’s place of business. (ii) Subject to the ‘Seven-Day Right to Cancel,’ as set forth in paragraph (7). (iii) Subject to licensure under the Alarm Company Act ..."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(6)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, when the Three/Five-Day Right to Cancel notice is required and its exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "“Three-Day Right to Cancel: You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor’s place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice. ... If you cancel, the contractor must return to you anything you paid within 10 days of receiving the notice of cancellation.”"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(6)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, text of the statutory Three-Day Right to Cancel notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  "The following notice entitled “Seven-Day Right to Cancel” shall be provided to the buyer for any contract that is written for the repair or restoration of residential premises damaged by any sudden or catastrophic event for which a state of emergency has been declared by the President of the United States or the Governor, or for which a local emergency has been declared ..."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159(e)(7)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, the Seven-Day Right to Cancel for declared-disaster repair contracts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's cancellation-notice requirement for a home improvement contract signed away from the contractor's place of business — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contract's cancellation rights. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159(e)(6) and (e)(7)) rather than independently authored sources. It doesn't state how 'contractor's place of business' is determined on disputed facts, and a separate body of law (Civil Code sections 1689.5 to 1689.14, not researched for this clause) governs the mechanics of exercising this cancellation right in more detail.

HOME IMPROVEMENT CONTRACT — THREE-DAY RIGHT TO CANCEL NOTICE
YOUR RIGHT TO CANCEL

Three-Day Right to Cancel

You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor's place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice. Include your name, your address, and the date you received the signed copy of the contract and this notice.

If you cancel, the contractor must return to you anything you paid within 10 days of receiving the notice of cancellation. For your part, you must make available to the contractor at your residence, in substantially as good condition as you received them, goods delivered to you under this contract or sale. Or, you may, if you wish, comply with the contractor's instructions on how to return the goods at the contractor's expense and risk. If you do make the goods available to the contractor and the contractor does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may keep them without any further obligation. If you fail to make the goods available to the contractor, or if you agree to return the goods to the contractor and fail to do so, then you remain liable for performance of all obligations under the contract.

(If the buyer is a senior citizen, references above to "three" and "third" become "five" and "fifth," respectively.)

Contractor's Name: Acme Construction, Inc.
Contractor's Address (for sending this notice): _______________________________________________
Contractor's Email Address: _______________________________________________
Contractor's Telephone Number: _______________________________________________

Owner's acknowledgment of receipt (sign and date):
Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —
NOTICE OF CANCELLATION

_______________________
(Date of Transaction)

You may cancel this transaction, without any penalty or obligation, within three business days from the above date.

If you cancel, any property traded in, any payments made by you under the contract or sale, and any negotiable instrument executed by you will be returned within 10 days following receipt by the seller of your cancellation notice, and any security interest arising out of the transaction will be canceled.

If you cancel, you must make available to the seller at your residence, in substantially as good condition as when received, any goods delivered to you under this contract or sale, or you may, if you wish, comply with the instructions of the seller regarding the return shipment of the goods at the seller's expense and risk.

If you do make the goods available to the seller and the seller does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may retain or dispose of the goods without any further obligation. If you fail to make the goods available to the seller, or if you agree to return the goods to the seller and fail to do so, then you remain liable for performance of all obligations under the contract.

To cancel this transaction, email, mail, or deliver a signed and dated copy of this cancellation notice, or any other written notice, to:

Acme Construction, Inc., at _______________________________________________ (contractor's place of business), not later than midnight of _______________________ (date).

I hereby cancel this transaction.

Date: _______________
Buyer's Signature: _______________________________________________

CONSEQUENCES OF CONTRACTING WITHOUT A LICENSE: § 7031
The Contractors State License Law attaches significant consequences to contracting without a license. With limited exceptions, a person acting as a contractor may not bring or maintain any court action to recover compensation for work requiring a license unless that person alleges — and, if licensure is disputed, proves with a verified certificate of licensure from the Contractors State License Board — that they were duly licensed at all times while performing the work, regardless of the merits of the underlying claim. Separately, and just as significantly, a person who used an unlicensed contractor's services may bring a court action to recover all compensation paid to that unlicensed contractor for the work. A security interest taken to secure payment for work requiring a license is unenforceable if the person who did the work was not duly licensed throughout. A narrow judicial 'substantial compliance' exception can excuse a licensing lapse in limited circumstances — where the person had been duly licensed before doing the work, acted reasonably and in good faith to keep the license current, and acted promptly and in good faith to fix the lapse once aware of it — but that exception is unavailable to someone who was never licensed in California at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), no person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a contractor, may bring or maintain any action, or recover in law or equity in any action, in any court of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any act or contract where a license is required by this chapter without alleging that they were a duly licensed contractor at all times during the performance of that act or contract, regardless of the merits of the cause of action brought by the person ..."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, bar on an unlicensed contractor recovering compensation in court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7031.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), a person who utilizes the services of an unlicensed contractor may bring an action in any court of competent jurisdiction in this state to recover all compensation paid to the unlicensed contractor for performance of any act or contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, homeowner's right to recover all compensation paid to an unlicensed contractor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7031.)
  "The judicial doctrine of substantial compliance shall not apply under this section where the person who engaged in the business or acted in the capacity of a contractor has never been a duly licensed contractor in this state. However ... the court may determine that there has been substantial compliance with licensure requirements under this section if it is shown at an evidentiary hearing that the person ... (1) had been duly licensed as a contractor in this state prior to the performance of the act or contract, (2) acted reasonably and in good faith to maintain proper licensure, and (3) acted promptly and in good faith to remedy the failure to comply with the licensure requirements upon learning of the failure."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, narrow substantial-compliance exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7031.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual consequences California attaches to unlicensed contracting — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular contractor's licensure or a particular homeowner's remedies. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7031) rather than independently authored sources. It doesn't state whether a specific person was required to be licensed for specific work, whether a specific person's licensure is genuinely disputed, or how a court would apply the narrow substantial-compliance exception on particular facts.

THE NARROWER 'SERVICE AND REPAIR CONTRACT' CATEGORY, AND WHEN IT DOESN'T APPLY
Not every small home-repair job is a "home improvement contract" subject to the full requirements described elsewhere in this document. California law separately defines a narrower "service and repair contract" category, but only where every one of several conditions is met: the contract amount is $750 or less; the buyer — not the contractor — initiated contact requesting the work; the contractor doesn't sell the buyer goods or services beyond what's reasonably necessary to address the specific problem that prompted the call; and no payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed. If a contract is written as, or presented to the buyer as, a service and repair contract but any one of those conditions isn't actually met, the full home improvement contract requirements apply instead, regardless of the contract's dollar amount — including whatever right to rescind would otherwise apply. A contract that genuinely qualifies has its own separate, shorter disclosure list (its own required insurance notices and its own right-to-cancel notice), but does not need a down-payment or progress-payment schedule, since payment isn't permitted until the work is done.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Service and repair contract” means an agreement ... that conforms to the following requirements: (A) The contract amount is seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or less. (B) The prospective buyer initiated contact with the contractor to request the work. (C) The contractor does not sell the buyer goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem that caused the buyer to contact the contractor. (D) No payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, definition and conditions of a qualifying 'service and repair contract' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.10.)
  "For any contract written pursuant to subdivision (a) or otherwise presented to the buyer as a service and repair contract, unless all of the conforming requirements for service and repair contracts specified in subdivision (a) are met, the contract requirements for home improvements set forth in subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of Section 7159 shall be applicable, including any rights to rescind the contract ... regardless of the aggregate contract price."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code, fallback to full home improvement contract requirements when the conditions aren't met (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7159.10.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California treats a small, buyer-initiated repair call as a distinct, more lightly regulated contract category from a full home improvement contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular repair job. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159.10) rather than independently authored sources. Note for this project specifically: the meaningful HIC-versus-service-and-repair distinction lives in section 7159.10, not section 7159.5 — section 7159.5 instead states payment-related rules (down payment cap, prohibition on paying for incomplete work) that apply to every home improvement contract; it was worth checking directly rather than assumed, and the two sections should not be conflated. This clause doesn't state whether a particular job in fact meets every element of the statutory definition.

HOME IMPROVEMENT CONTRACT — MECHANICS LIEN WARNING AND CSLB NOTICE
MECHANICS LIEN WARNING

Anyone who helps improve your property, but who is not paid, may record what is called a mechanics lien on your property. A mechanics lien is a claim, like a mortgage or home equity loan, made against your property and recorded with the county recorder.

Even if you pay your contractor in full, unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, and laborers who helped to improve your property may record mechanics liens and sue you in court to foreclose the lien. If a court finds the lien is valid, you could be forced to pay twice or have a court officer sell your home to pay the lien. Liens can also affect your credit.

To preserve their right to record a lien, each subcontractor and material supplier must provide you with a document called a 'Preliminary Notice.' This notice is not a lien. The purpose of the notice is to let you know that the person who sends you the notice has the right to record a lien on your property if they are not paid.

BE CAREFUL. The Preliminary Notice can be sent up to 20 days after the subcontractor starts work or the supplier provides material. This can be a big problem if you pay your contractor before you have received the Preliminary Notices.

You will not get Preliminary Notices from your prime contractor or from laborers who work on your project. The law assumes that you already know they are improving your property.

PROTECT YOURSELF FROM LIENS. You can protect yourself from liens by getting a list from your contractor of all the subcontractors and material suppliers that work on your project. Find out from your contractor when these subcontractors started work and when these suppliers delivered goods or materials. Then wait 20 days, paying attention to the Preliminary Notices you receive.

PAY WITH JOINT CHECKS. One way to protect yourself is to pay with a joint check. When your contractor tells you it is time to pay for the work of a subcontractor or supplier who has provided you with a Preliminary Notice, write a joint check payable to both the contractor and the subcontractor or material supplier.

For other ways to prevent liens, visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov or call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752).

REMEMBER, IF YOU DO NOTHING, YOU RISK HAVING A LIEN PLACED ON YOUR HOME. This can mean that you may have to pay twice, or face the forced sale of your home to pay what you owe.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Information about the Contractors State License Board (CSLB): CSLB is the state consumer protection agency that licenses and regulates construction contractors.

Contact CSLB for information about the licensed contractor you are considering, including information about disclosable complaints, disciplinary actions, and civil judgments that are reported to CSLB.

Use only licensed contractors. If you file a complaint against a licensed contractor within the legal deadline (usually four years), CSLB has authority to investigate the complaint. If you use an unlicensed contractor, CSLB may not be able to help you resolve your complaint. Your only remedy may be in civil court, and you may be liable for damages arising out of any injuries to the unlicensed contractor or the unlicensed contractor's employees.

For more information:
Visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov
Call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752)
Write CSLB at P.O. Box 26000, Sacramento, CA 95826.

Contractor's License Number: 123456

California's Contractors State License Law defines a "home improvement contract" as an agreement — oral or written, in one or more documents — between a contractor and a homeowner (or, in some cases, a tenant) for a home improvement as statutorily defined, where the aggregate contract price exceeds $500. Once that threshold is met, the contract and any changes to it must be in writing and signed by the parties before work covered by the contract (or a change order) begins. Before any work starts, the contractor must give the buyer a copy of the signed, dated contract, and the buyer's receipt of that copy is what starts the buyer's statutory cancellation-notice period running. The written contract must include, among other things, the contractor's name, business address, and license number; a "Home Improvement" heading; a "Contract Price" heading with the amount in dollars and cents; a description of the project and the significant materials and equipment involved; headings for the approximate start date and approximate completion date; and, in close proximity to the signatures, a notice that the owner or tenant has the right to require the contractor to carry a performance and payment bond. A change-order or extra-work form becomes part of the contract only if it is a separate writing signed by the parties before the change-order work begins. Beyond these core terms, the contract (or an attachment it references) must include several specific disclosure notices: a commercial general liability insurance (CGL) notice stating, correctly, whether the contractor carries CGL insurance, is self-insured, or carries the liability coverage the law requires; a workers' compensation insurance notice stating whether the contractor has no employees and is exempt, or carries coverage for all employees; a "Mechanics Lien Warning" in specific statutory language, telling the owner that even a contractor who has been paid in full may leave unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, or laborers who can still record a lien on the property; and a notice with the Contractors State License Board's (CSLB) contact information, cautioning the buyer that using an unlicensed contractor may leave the buyer's only remedy in civil court, with possible liability for injuries to the unlicensed contractor or that contractor's employees.

expectedJSON.body: California law caps the down payment a home improvement contract may require: if any down payment is charged, it may not exceed $1,000 or 10% of the contract price, whichever amount is less, and the contract must display that exact dollar/percentage cap in boldface type. Beyond the down payment, the contractor generally may neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work actually performed or the materials actually delivered — the schedule of progress payments must be stated in dollars and cents tied to specific phases of work, and the contract must include a boldface statement that it is against the law to collect payment for work not yet completed or materials not yet delivered. A contractor who instead furnishes a qualifying performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, or an approved joint control is exempt from the down-payment cap and the progress-payment restrictions, and may accept payment before the work is completed. Violating the writing requirement, the down-payment cap, or the rule against accepting payment beyond the value of work performed is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $100 nor more than $5,000, by up to one year in county jail, or by both.

YOUR RIGHT TO CANCEL

Three-Day Right to Cancel

You, the buyer, have the right to cancel this contract within three business days. You may cancel by emailing, mailing, faxing, or delivering a written notice to the contractor at the contractor's place of business by midnight of the third business day after you received a signed and dated copy of the contract that includes this notice. Include your name, your address, and the date you received the signed copy of the contract and this notice.

If you cancel, the contractor must return to you anything you paid within 10 days of receiving the notice of cancellation. For your part, you must make available to the contractor at your residence, in substantially as good condition as you received them, goods delivered to you under this contract or sale. Or, you may, if you wish, comply with the contractor's instructions on how to return the goods at the contractor's expense and risk. If you do make the goods available to the contractor and the contractor does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may keep them without any further obligation. If you fail to make the goods available to the contractor, or if you agree to return the goods to the contractor and fail to do so, then you remain liable for performance of all obligations under the contract.

(If the buyer is a senior citizen, references above to "three" and "third" become "five" and "fifth," respectively.)

If you do make the goods available to the seller and the seller does not pick them up within 20 days of the date of your notice of cancellation, you may retain or dispose of the goods without any further obligation. The Contractors State License Law attaches significant consequences to contracting without a license. With limited exceptions, a person acting as a contractor may not bring or maintain any court action to recover compensation for work requiring a license unless that person alleges — and, if licensure is disputed, proves with a verified certificate of licensure from the Contractors State License Board — that they were duly licensed at all times while performing the work, regardless of the merits of the underlying claim. Separately, and just as significantly, a person who used an unlicensed contractor's services may bring a court action to recover all compensation paid to that unlicensed contractor for the work. A security interest taken to secure payment for work requiring a license is unenforceable if the person who did the work was not duly licensed throughout. A narrow judicial 'substantial compliance' exception can excuse a licensing lapse in limited circumstances — where the person had been duly licensed before doing the work, acted reasonably and in good faith to keep the license current, and acted promptly and in good faith to fix the lapse once aware of it — but that exception is unavailable to someone who was never licensed in California at all.

expectedJSON.body: Not every small home-repair job is a "home improvement contract" subject to the full requirements described elsewhere in this document. California law separately defines a narrower "service and repair contract" category, but only where every one of several conditions is met: the contract amount is $750 or less; the buyer — not the contractor — initiated contact requesting the work; the contractor doesn't sell the buyer goods or services beyond what's reasonably necessary to address the specific problem that prompted the call; and no payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed. If a contract is written as, or presented to the buyer as, a service and repair contract but any one of those conditions isn't actually met, the full home improvement contract requirements apply instead, regardless of the contract's dollar amount — including whatever right to rescind would otherwise apply. A contract that genuinely qualifies has its own separate, shorter disclosure list (its own required insurance notices and its own right-to-cancel notice), but does not need a down-payment or progress-payment schedule, since payment isn't permitted until the work is done.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition and conditions of a qualifying 'service and repair contract'
citations.quote: “Service and repair contract” means an agreement ... that conforms to the following requirements: (A) The contract amount is seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or less. (B) The prospective buyer initiated contact with the contractor to request the work. (C) The contractor does not sell the buyer goods or services beyond those reasonably necessary to take care of the particular problem that caused the buyer to contact the contractor. (D) No payment is due, or accepted by the contractor, until the work is completed.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7159.10(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, fallback to full home improvement contract requirements when the conditions aren't met
citations.quote: For any contract written pursuant to subdivision (a) or otherwise presented to the buyer as a service and repair contract, unless all of the conforming requirements for service and repair contracts specified in subdivision (a) are met, the contract requirements for home improvements set forth in subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of Section 7159 shall be applicable, including any rights to rescind the contract ... regardless of the aggregate contract price.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California treats a small, buyer-initiated repair call as a distinct, more lightly regulated contract category from a full home improvement contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular repair job. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Bus. & Prof. Code section 7159.10) rather than independently authored sources. Note for this project specifically: the meaningful HIC-versus-service-and-repair distinction lives in section 7159.10, not section 7159.5 — section 7159.5 instead states payment-related rules (down payment cap, prohibition on paying for incomplete work) that apply to every home improvement contract; it was worth checking directly rather than assumed, and the two sections should not be conflated. This clause doesn't state whether a particular job in fact meets every element of the statutory definition.

expectedJSON.body:
MECHANICS LIEN WARNING

Anyone who helps improve your property, but who is not paid, may record what is called a mechanics lien on your property. A mechanics lien is a claim, like a mortgage or home equity loan, made against your property and recorded with the county recorder.

Even if you pay your contractor in full, unpaid subcontractors, suppliers, and laborers who helped to improve your property may record mechanics liens and sue you in court to foreclose the lien. If a court finds the lien is valid, you could be forced to pay twice or have a court officer sell your home to pay the lien. Liens can also affect your credit.

To preserve their right to record a lien, each subcontractor and material supplier must provide you with a document called a 'Preliminary Notice.' This notice is not a lien. The purpose of the notice is to let you know that the person who sends you the notice has the right to record a lien on your property if they are not paid.

BE CAREFUL. The Preliminary Notice can be sent up to 20 days after the subcontractor starts work or the supplier provides material. This can be a big problem if you pay your contractor before you have received the Preliminary Notices.

You will not get Preliminary Notices from your prime contractor or from laborers who work on your project. The law assumes that you already know they are improving your property.

PROTECT YOURSELF FROM LIENS. You can protect yourself from liens by getting a list from your contractor of all the subcontractors and material suppliers that work on your project. Find out from your contractor when these subcontractors started work and when these suppliers delivered goods or materials. Then wait 20 days, paying attention to the Preliminary Notices you receive.

PAY WITH JOINT CHECKS. One way to protect yourself is to pay with a joint check. When your contractor tells you it is time to pay for the work of a subcontractor or supplier who has provided you with a Preliminary Notice, write a joint check payable to both the contractor and the subcontractor or material supplier.

For other ways to prevent liens, visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov or call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752).

REMEMBER, IF YOU DO NOTHING, YOU RISK HAVING A LIEN PLACED ON YOUR HOME. This can mean that you may have to pay twice, or face the forced sale of your home to pay what you owe.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Information about the Contractors State License Board (CSLB): CSLB is the state consumer protection agency that licenses and regulates construction contractors.

Contact CSLB for information about the licensed contractor you are considering, including information about disclosable complaints, disciplinary actions, and civil judgments that are reported to CSLB.

Use only licensed contractors. If you file a complaint against a licensed contractor within the legal deadline (usually four years), CSLB has authority to investigate the complaint. If you use an unlicensed contractor, CSLB may not be able to help you resolve your complaint. Your only remedy may be in civil court, and you may be liable for damages arising out of any injuries to the unlicensed contractor or the unlicensed contractor's employees.

For more information:
Visit CSLB's internet website at www.cslb.ca.gov
Call CSLB at 800-321-CSLB (2752)
Write CSLB at P.O. Box 26000, Sacramento, CA 95826.
